actionHint: Note the unsaved change and check device storage, then restart. Do not clear local data.
summary: This change could not be saved to the local database and remains only on this device.
docsBody: Do not clear or reload local data. Export diagnostics and contact support before retrying or repairing anything.
troubleshooting: If the log entry names a record, note it — that is the change that has not been saved. Site and credential writes may name only the failed operation and error instead; record those details before continuing.
Do not clear site data, reset the app, or uninstall: the unsaved change exists only on this device, and clearing local storage deletes it permanently.
Check the device's free storage — a full disk or an exhausted browser storage quota is the most common reason a local write fails.
Restart WCPOS once and make a small, harmless edit to confirm whether new changes save.
If writes keep failing, use Copy debug info on the Logs screen and contact support before attempting any repair.

actionHint: Repair from Store health → Database.
summary: Local store data is damaged and needs repair before syncing can continue.
docsBody: Run the targeted repair for the affected data, and reset that local data only if the problem returns.
troubleshooting: Open Store health → Database and run the targeted repair for the affected data; a full reset discards more than the repair does.
Retry the action that failed, then watch Store health → Logs for a repeat of this code.
If the same data is flagged again, reset just that local data so it downloads fresh from your store — but only after any unsent changes have been noted.
Corruption that keeps returning points at failing device storage: export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Keep working — sync resumes when the store is reachable.
summary: Your store cannot be reached right now, so changes will stay on this device.
docsBody: Check the connection and keep working offline; syncing will retry automatically when the store is reachable.
troubleshooting: Keep selling — sales are saved on this device and sync resumes automatically once the store answers.
Check whether the till itself is online: can any other website load from this device?
Open your store's own website in a browser tab on the same device; if it does not load there either, the site or its hosting is down, not the POS.
If the site loads but the POS stays offline, something between the two is blocking API requests — a VPN, firewall, ad-blocker or security plugin; the network inspector shows which request fails.

actionHint: Ask the site admin to check the server logs, then retry.
summary: Your store returned an error, so this action did not complete.
docsBody: The store was reached but its server failed to handle the request. This is a problem on the website rather than the POS, so retrying alone may not help: check the site's error log or ask the host to, then retry. Nothing was lost on this device.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry and note the status, endpoint and serverCode — they say what the server was doing when it failed.
Open WooCommerce → Status → Logs on the site and check the newest fatal-errors log around the failure time; a 500-class response almost always leaves a PHP error there.
If the failure started after a plugin, theme or PHP update on the site, suspect that change first and roll it back or disable it.
If WooCommerce's logs show nothing, ask the hosting provider for the server's PHP error log for the same time window.
Once the server-side cause is fixed, retry from the POS — the change is still saved on this device.
evidence: private mining SY02002+500; woocommerce-pos#572 (critical error on this website); woocommerce-pos#571 (PHP fatal, disk full)

actionHint: Wait — WCPOS retries automatically.
summary: Your store is limiting requests temporarily, so this action will retry later.
docsBody: Wait before retrying. If rate limits continue, ask the site administrator or host to review the store's request limits.
troubleshooting: Wait — the POS backs off and retries by itself; retrying by hand only extends the throttle.
Nothing needs to be re-entered: the affected changes stay on the device and go through on a later attempt.

If the code keeps appearing, ask the site administrator to find which layer returns the 429 — a security plugin, a CDN or firewall rule, or the host's own limits — and to allow the POS's REST traffic.
The expanded log entry's endpoint and timestamps help the administrator match the throttle in their own dashboards.

actionHint: Fix the field the store refused, then retry.
summary: This record was rejected by your store and is saved only on this device.
docsBody: Correct the reason shown for the named record, then retry it. Export diagnostics if it remains rejected.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry: it names the rejected record and carries the store's own reason (serverCode) for refusing it.
Rejected records are listed in Store health — open the record, correct the detail the store refused, and retry it from there.
If the reason mentions a field the POS does not show, open the same record in WP Admin and check it there — another plugin may have added validation the POS cannot see.
If it stays rejected after editing, use Copy debug info and contact support, including the serverCode.

actionHint: Fix the named field, then retry.
summary: This record has a field your store will not accept.
docsBody: Fix the named field and retry the record; the local copy remains available until it syncs.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry and check the endpoint and server response first: this code can also represent an HTTP 400 from a settings, authentication or other non-record request.
If the context names a record or field, edit that field in the POS — common causes are a value out of range, a rejected format or a required option left empty — then retry.
If it is not a record request, follow the server's message for the named endpoint instead. Use the Network inspector when the response details are not present in the POS log.
If a named field looks correct in the POS, compare it with the same record in WP Admin: plugin-added validation on the store can reject values the POS considers fine.

actionHint: Download the affected data again.
summary: Some older store changes were skipped and must be downloaded again.
docsBody: Run a targeted download for the affected data and export diagnostics if the gap remains.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry — its context records how far behind the till fell and whether changes were skipped.
Run a targeted download for the affected data so the skipped store changes are fetched again.
Afterwards, spot-check a few recently-edited records against WP Admin to confirm the gap closed.
If the gap reappears, export debug info and contact support rather than resetting anything.

actionHint: Clear the local database and reopen. This loses any unsynced sales.
summary: Local data is from an incompatible version and cannot open yet.
docsBody: Do not reset the affected local collection when this device may hold changes that never reached your store — resetting deletes the only local copy. Export diagnostics to help support investigate, then contact support for recovery guidance.
troubleshooting: Do not reset or delete the affected collection — if this device holds changes that never reached the store, the local copy is the only copy.
Check whether the app was recently updated or downgraded on this device; a version mismatch between the app and its stored data is the usual trigger.
Update WCPOS to the newest version on this device and reopen the store.
If the collection still will not open, use Copy debug info and contact support for recovery guidance before touching local data.

actionHint: Retry only the records that failed.
summary: Some records synced, but one or more records did not.
docsBody: Review the named records and their reasons before retrying only the records that did not sync.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry to list which records did not sync and the reason each one gives.
Handle each named record by its own reason — an invalid field needs editing, a conflict needs comparing with the store.
Retry only the records that failed; the rest are already synced and need nothing.

actionHint: Download the affected records again.
summary: This record on the device does not match your store and needs local repair.
docsBody: Nothing you entered is waiting to be sent. The device's copy of a record your store owns has drifted from the store's copy; repair it according to the status shown in the log.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry - its context names the collection, the record id, the status and the detector that spotted the difference.
For a changed or missing record, run a targeted download for the affected collection so the device replaces its copy with the store's.
For a deleted record, remove the local copy; the server tombstone must not be downloaded.
Compare the record in WP Admin with what the POS shows; a price or stock difference is the visible symptom.

If the SAME records keep reappearing after repair, the store's stored digests are stale - this happens after a bulk write that skips WooCommerce's save hooks (a CSV import, a migration plugin, WP-CLI or direct SQL). The record itself is usually fine; a site administrator can clear it by rebuilding the integrity index, and WCPOS schedules that rebuild automatically once a range keeps reporting the same difference.
If it still returns after a rebuild, export debug info and contact support.
evidence: monorepo: dev-pro session 2026-08-19, 138 products escalated per sweep

actionHint: Update the POS app on this device, then reopen it.
summary: This store now requires a newer version of the POS app.
docsBody: The store's WCPOS plugin has moved to a newer sync protocol than this app speaks, and the server deliberately pauses syncing until the app is updated — this protects the store's data from being read or written incorrectly. Nothing on the till is lost: sales and edits waiting to be sent stay safely on the device and sync once an updated app connects. On the web app, reload the page to pick up the new version; on desktop and mobile, install the app update and reopen it.
troubleshooting: On the web app, reload the browser tab — the web app picks up the new version on reload. If the screen comes back, use a hard reload (hold Shift while reloading).
On desktop, install the pending update and reopen the app — the check runs when the app reconnects. If no update is offered, download the latest build from the installation guide at docs.wcpos.com.

On iPhone, iPad or Android, update WCPOS through the channel you installed it from (TestFlight on iOS, the Play testing programme on Android — both linked from the installation guide), then reopen the app.

Site administrator: if no newer app is available yet, the store's WCPOS plugin was updated ahead of the matching app release. Restoring the previous WCPOS plugin version on the store resumes syncing until the newer app ships.
If neither an app update nor a plugin rollback is available to you, contact WCPOS support.
evidence: deliberate 426 wcpos_update_required gate refusal (wcpos/woocommerce-pos#1752); client signal monorepo#1599

actionHint: Sign in again.
summary: Your session ended and you need to sign in again.
docsBody: Sign in again and repeat the request; no local data was lost.
troubleshooting: Sign in again when prompted, then repeat the action — nothing on the till was lost.
Frequent expiries (several per day) usually come from the site: a security plugin shortening session lifetimes or clearing tokens. Ask the site administrator which security plugins run on the store.

actionHint: Ask your store admin to grant your account POS access.
summary: Your account does not have permission to perform this action.
docsBody: Ask a store administrator to grant the required POS capability, then try again.
troubleshooting: Note which action was refused — the log entry records the request and the permission check that failed.
Ask a store administrator to review the account's role: POS cashiers need the POS capabilities WCPOS registers, and role-editing plugins can strip them.
After the role is corrected, sign out and back in on the till, then try again.

actionHint: Ask the site admin to exempt WCPOS in the conflicting auth plugin.
summary: Another authentication plugin is preventing WCPOS from connecting.
docsBody: Ask the site administrator to resolve the named plugin conflict before signing in again.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry — it names the conflicting plugin where the store reports it.
Ask the site administrator to review that plugin's settings: most authentication plugins can exempt the WCPOS REST routes instead of being disabled outright.
After the change, sign in again from the till.
If it is unclear which plugin conflicts, test on a staging copy by disabling security and login plugins one at a time.

actionHint: Ask the site admin to check WCPOS is active and REST isn't blocked.
summary: The WCPOS store route is unavailable.
docsBody: Ask the site administrator to check whether a security or proxy plugin is stripping WCPOS request headers.
troubleshooting: Confirm WCPOS is active on the site: WP Admin → Plugins.
Test both supported REST forms in a browser: your store's /wp-json/ address and /index.php?rest_route=/. Only diagnose a REST block if neither address returns JSON.

If neither REST form works, ask the site administrator whether a security plugin, proxy or CDN is stripping WCPOS request headers or blocking REST requests — firewall rules and disable-REST-API hardening options are the usual culprits.
On some hosts, re-saving permalinks (Settings → Permalinks → Save) restores missing REST routes.

actionHint: Check the store address; ask the admin to fix the site's certificate.
summary: A secure connection to this store could not be trusted.
docsBody: Use the correct store address and ask the site administrator to repair the certificate before reconnecting.
troubleshooting: Open the store address in a browser on the same device — the browser's padlock or warning page shows exactly what is wrong with the certificate (expired, self-signed, or issued for a different domain).
Check the address the POS uses: https:// and the exact domain the certificate covers — with or without www matters.
Ask the site administrator or host to renew or fix the certificate; an automatic renewal silently failing is the most common cause.
Do not work around a certificate warning by disabling security — fix the certificate.

actionHint: Review the cart and try checkout again.
summary: Checkout did not finish, and the cart is still safe to retry.
docsBody: Review the cart and retry checkout; the current cart contents have been preserved.
troubleshooting: Review the cart — it is unchanged — and try checkout again.
If it fails the same way, expand the log entry: the serverCode and status say whether the store refused the order and why.
A repeated failure with a 500-class status is a site problem — check WooCommerce → Status → Logs for a PHP error at the failure time.
If the reason names a specific line item, remove it, complete the sale, and investigate that product afterwards.

actionHint: Check whether the order exists before retrying. Do not re-charge.
summary: WCPOS could not confirm whether checkout completed.
docsBody: Do not retry blindly. Check the store for the order first, then export diagnostics if its outcome is still unclear.
troubleshooting: Do not retry checkout yet, and do not charge the customer again.
Open WooCommerce → Orders in WP Admin and look for the order — search by the total and the last few minutes.
If the order exists, the sale went through — do not create it again; sync the POS so it appears on the till.
If no order exists after a sync, retry checkout once.
Still unclear? Export debug info and contact support before another attempt.

actionHint: Check whether the order exists before retrying. Do not re-charge.
summary: The store returned no checkout result, so the order status is unknown.
docsBody: Check whether the order was created before trying checkout again.
troubleshooting: Check WooCommerce → Orders in WP Admin before doing anything else — an empty response often means the order was created but the confirmation never arrived.
The network inspector shows the checkout request: a success status with an empty or truncated body points at a plugin or server buffer cutting the response short.
Check WooCommerce → Status → Logs for a fatal error during checkout — a PHP crash after the order is created produces exactly this.
Only retry checkout once you have confirmed no order was created.
evidence: Discord: Empty response from server x15

actionHint: Remove the item to finish the sale; ask the admin to fix its SKU.
summary: Checkout cannot continue because a product SKU is duplicated or invalid.
docsBody: Change or remove the named SKU, then retry with the preserved cart.
troubleshooting: The log entry names the SKU the store refused.
In WP Admin, search Products for that SKU — two products, or a product and a variation, share it. Give each one a unique SKU.
Back on the till, retry checkout — the cart is preserved.

actionHint: No action needed — the payment succeeded; reopen to refresh.
summary: Payment succeeded, but WCPOS could not refresh its status afterward.
docsBody: The payment completed and should not be charged again; no action is required unless the displayed status stays stale.
troubleshooting: No action is needed — the payment completed; only the follow-up status refresh failed.
Do not charge the customer again.
If the order's status looks stale on the till, reopen or sync the order; the store already has the correct status.

actionHint: Check the terminal and provider dashboard before re-charging.
summary: WCPOS could not confirm whether the terminal charged the payment.
docsBody: Check the payment terminal before attempting another charge, and contact the payment provider if the result remains unclear.
troubleshooting: Do not run the card again yet.
Check the terminal's own screen, then your payment provider's dashboard — the provider's record is the authority on whether the charge went through.
Check the order in WP Admin: a payment that succeeded may already be recorded there.
Only take payment again once the provider's dashboard shows no charge.
If the charge shows as pending or uncertain, contact the payment provider before acting.
evidence: email: terminal charged but POS stuck

actionHint: Take another payment method; ask the admin to check the gateway.
summary: The selected payment gateway is unavailable for this store.
docsBody: Ask the site administrator to verify that the gateway is supported, enabled, and correctly configured.
troubleshooting: Ask the site administrator to check the gateway in WooCommerce → Settings → Payments: it must be installed, enabled, and enabled for POS use in the POS settings.
Complete the sale meanwhile with another method, such as cash.
If the gateway worked yesterday, check whether it or WooCommerce updated — WooCommerce → Status → Logs records gateway initialization errors.

actionHint: Wake the terminal, check its connection, and re-pair.
summary: The payment terminal did not finish pairing with WCPOS.
docsBody: Retry pairing after checking the terminal settings, and include the trace ID when contacting the payment provider.
troubleshooting: Restart the pairing from the terminal settings, keeping the terminal awake and on the same network as the till.
Check the basics first: terminal charged, connected to the right network or Bluetooth, and not still paired to another till.
The log entry carries a trace ID — include it when contacting the payment provider if pairing still will not complete.

actionHint: Print the receipt manually.
summary: Automatic printing did not start for this receipt.
docsBody: Check the selected printer, template, and connection, then use Print now to print the receipt manually.
troubleshooting: Use Print now to print the receipt by hand — the sale is unaffected.
Check the printing settings: the right printer is selected and a receipt template is chosen.
If auto-print fails on every sale, note whether manual printing works — manual-works-but-auto-fails is a settings problem; both failing is a printer problem.

actionHint: Check the printer before reprinting.
summary: WCPOS could not confirm that the print job completed.
docsBody: Check the printer before retrying so the receipt is not printed twice.
troubleshooting: Look at the printer before retrying — the job may have printed even though no confirmation came back, and a blind retry prints the receipt twice.
Check paper, covers and error lights on the printer.
If nothing printed, retry once from the order's receipt screen.
For repeated failures, power-cycle the printer and check its connection to the till.

actionHint: Check the printer's power, cable, and network.
summary: The selected printer cannot be reached.
docsBody: Check that the printer is powered on and connected, then try printing again.
troubleshooting: Check the printer is powered on and its cable or network connection is seated.
For network printers, confirm the till and printer are on the same network and the printer's address has not changed — DHCP renewals can move it.
Print a self-test from the printer itself to confirm the hardware works, then try again from the POS.
If the printer's address changed, update it in the POS printing settings.

actionHint: Fix the reported cause, then retry.
summary: This product could not be saved to your store.
docsBody: Review the reported cause before retrying: reconnect for a network error, fix invalid fields, or refresh a conflicting product.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry — the error text usually shows whether this was a network failure, a field the store rejected, or a conflicting edit made in the store.
Network failure: check the connection and retry; the edit is kept on this device.
Rejected field: correct the named field and retry.
Conflicting edit: open the product in WP Admin, compare versions, and re-apply the correct values.
If saves keep failing with no clear reason, export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Fix the variation fields, then retry.
summary: This variation could not be added to the product.
docsBody: Review and correct the variation fields, then retry; export diagnostics if it is still rejected.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry for the store's reason (serverCode) — usually a missing attribute or an invalid option combination.
Check the parent product's attributes in WP Admin: every attribute the variation uses must exist on the parent and be marked as used for variations.
Correct the variation's fields and retry.
Still rejected? Export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Keep selling — the image retries in the background.
summary: This product image is unavailable, but the product can still be sold.
docsBody: Continue the sale without the image; WCPOS will try to load it again later.
troubleshooting: Sell as normal — the product is unaffected and the image is retried in the background.
If one product's image never loads, open the product in WP Admin and re-save its image; the file may have been removed from the media library.
If many images fail at once, the site's media hosting or CDN is the cause — check whether images load on the store website itself.

actionHint: Clear the filters, or search by name.
summary: No products matched the current search and filters.
docsBody: Review spaces, category filters, and whether the local product index has finished syncing before searching again.
troubleshooting: The scanned code is placed in the search box, so start with the filters: a category or stock filter silently narrows every search.
Look the product up by name — if it appears, its barcode field in the store does not contain the scanned value; add the barcode to the product in WP Admin.
Check the barcode field in the POS barcode settings — if your store keeps barcodes in a different field, the POS reads the wrong one and every scan misses.
If the product is brand new, the local index may still be syncing: give the first sync time to finish, then scan again.

actionHint: Confirm real stock before selling low-stock items.
summary: The displayed stock may be older than the store stock.
docsBody: Verify current stock in the store before completing a sale that could oversell the item.
troubleshooting: Before selling a low-stock item, check its live stock in WP Admin — the till's number may be older than the store's.
Stale stock usually means sync has been failing or paused: look for sync errors in Store health → Logs and fix those first.
After sync recovers, the stock display catches up on its own.

actionHint: Re-activate the license for this store in WP Admin.
summary: Your WCPOS Pro license is not active for this store or device.
docsBody: Check the local, licensing-server, and updater status, then activate the license for the named store.
troubleshooting: Check the license status in the POS settings in WP Admin — it should show active for this store's exact URL.
A site URL change (http to https, adding or dropping www, a domain move, a staging copy) deactivates the license for the new address — re-activate it for the current one.
If the license shows active but the POS disagrees, deactivate and re-activate once, then reload the till.
Still locked? Export debug info and contact support with your license reference.

actionHint: Update the WCPOS and Pro plugins to matching versions.
summary: WCPOS Pro is disabled because its version does not match WCPOS.
docsBody: Update the named WCPOS or WCPOS Pro component so both versions are compatible.
troubleshooting: Check both plugin versions in WP Admin → Plugins — the log entry names which of WCPOS and WCPOS Pro is behind.
Update the older one; updating both to the latest versions resolves the skew.
If Pro updates are not being offered, the updater may not be authorized (see LICENSE301) — fix that first, then update.

actionHint: Re-authorize the license so updates can download.
summary: The updater is not authorized to download WCPOS Pro updates.
docsBody: Re-authorize the updater for this store, then check for updates again.
troubleshooting: Re-enter or re-activate the license key in the POS settings so the updater can authenticate.
Check for updates again from WP Admin → Dashboard → Updates.
If authorization keeps failing, the site may be blocking outbound requests to the update server — ask the host whether outbound HTTPS is restricted.

actionHint: Restart; if it won't start, clear the local database. This loses any unsynced sales.
summary: WCPOS could not finish starting.
docsBody: Restart once, then export diagnostics with the app version and device engine if startup still fails.
troubleshooting: Restart the app once; on web, fully reload the tab.
If startup fails again, note the app version and the device — the browser console records the startup error even when the POS cannot show it.
Do not clear site data or reinstall to fix startup — a till with unsent sales loses them; contact support first.
Export debug info if the app gets far enough to open the Logs screen; otherwise contact support with the console error.

actionHint: Close other apps or tabs, then restart.
summary: WCPOS ran out of memory and could not finish the operation.
docsBody: Restart WCPOS and retry once; export diagnostics if the device runs out of memory again.
troubleshooting: Restart WCPOS and retry the action once.
Close other apps or browser tabs — the POS shares the device's memory with everything else running on it.
If a specific action reliably runs out of memory, note what it was and contact support with debug info.
If this happens daily on the same device, the device may be too small for the catalogue — report it so support can confirm.

actionHint: Restart, and install app and device updates.
summary: WCPOS stopped because of a device-level crash.
docsBody: Restart WCPOS and export diagnostics if the crash repeats.
troubleshooting: Restart WCPOS — the crash happened at device level, not in your data.
Install pending updates for the app and the device's operating system; native crashes are often already-fixed bugs.
If the crash repeats on the same action, export debug info and contact support, noting exactly what was tapped when it crashed.

actionHint: Retry once; report it with the log details if it repeats.
summary: WCPOS encountered an unexpected error.
docsBody: Try the action once more, then export diagnostics and contact support if it fails again.
troubleshooting: Try the action once more.
Expand the log entry and note the event code and context — a 999 code means the failure has no dedicated code yet, and this is the information that identifies it.
If it repeats, export debug info and contact support — reporting it is how the specific code gets minted.

actionHint: Check the log — retry if it queued, otherwise re-enter and save.
summary: Syncing hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: Your sales are safe on this device. Wait for the automatic retry; if this code keeps appearing, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Do not assume this code will retry. Expand the log entry first: if it confirms the mutation was already queued, WCPOS retries automatically, so leave it open and let the queue drain.
If the error says the engine resident is missing or the write failed before a mutation ID was returned, nothing was queued — return to that record or order and save it again.
Expand the log entry and note the event code and any serverCode: a 999 code means the specific cause has no dedicated code yet, so this context is exactly what support needs.
If the code keeps appearing, use Copy debug info and contact support — reporting it is how the specific code gets added.
evidence: coverage net (map #1136, A1.1): generic fallback = registry debt

actionHint: Try again; if it repeats, contact support with the log details.
summary: Signing in or staying signed in hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: Try the action once more. If it repeats, sign out and back in, then export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Try the action once more; if it fails again, sign out and back in.
Expand the log entry and note the event code and any serverCode — a 999 code means the cause has no dedicated code yet, and that context is what identifies it.
If it recurs, use Copy debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Check WooCommerce → Orders before retrying. Do not re-charge.
summary: Checkout hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: Check the order in your store admin before charging the customer again. Export diagnostics and contact support if the problem repeats.
troubleshooting: Check WooCommerce → Orders in WP Admin for the order before charging the customer again.
Expand the log entry and note the event code and any serverCode — this generic code means the cause has no dedicated code yet.
If it repeats, export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Confirm whether the payment went through before retrying.
summary: Payment handling hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: Confirm whether the payment went through before retrying. Export diagnostics and contact support if it is unclear.
troubleshooting: Confirm whether the payment went through before retrying: the terminal screen, the provider dashboard, and the order in WP Admin.
Expand the log entry for the event code and context — this generic code means the cause has no dedicated code yet.
If the outcome stays unclear or the code recurs, export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Repeat only the operation named in the log.
summary: Printing hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: Try printing again. If it keeps failing, reprint from the order screen and contact support with diagnostics.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry first and identify the failed operation — this code also covers receipt-email queue actions and receipt-template sync, not only physical printing.

Repeat only the operation named in the log. Reprint from the order screen only for a physical print attempt; retry or remove a queued email from Store health, and retry template sync by reopening the receipt screen while connected.
If that operation keeps failing, export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Try again; report it if it repeats.
summary: Loading or updating products hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: Try again. If product data still looks wrong afterwards, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Try again — most one-off product loading problems clear on retry.
If product data still looks wrong, expand the log entry for the event code and context; this generic code means the cause has no dedicated code yet.
Export debug info and contact support if it recurs.

actionHint: Keep working; re-enter the key or contact support if it persists.
summary: License checking hit an unexpected problem.
docsBody: The POS keeps working. If Pro features stay locked, re-enter your license key, then contact support.
troubleshooting: Keep working — the POS does not lock up over license checks.
If Pro features stay locked, re-enter the license key in the POS settings.
If that does not clear it, export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: Nothing to do — the task restarts automatically.
summary: A background sync task stopped unexpectedly before finishing.
docsBody: The POS restarts these tasks automatically and no order data is affected. If this code keeps appearing, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Nothing to do on first sight: the POS restarts the crashed background task automatically and no order data is involved.
If the code repeats within minutes, reload the app once so the sync engine starts clean.
If it still repeats, export debug info and contact support — a recurring task crash is an app defect worth reporting, not a store problem.

actionHint: Keep working; report it if it keeps happening.
summary: This device asked the store for data far more often than normal.
docsBody: Nothing was slowed down or blocked, and no order data is affected — this is a detection-only alarm. Sustained request floods usually indicate an app problem (a screen re-requesting the same data in a loop) rather than anything you did. If this code keeps appearing, export diagnostics and contact support so the loop can be found and fixed.
troubleshooting: Keep working — this is a detection-only alarm. WCPOS does not slow, queue or drop any request, and no order or product data is affected.
If the code appears once and stops, no action is needed. If it repeats, note which screen was open and which action you were taking when it appeared.
Use Copy debug info while the event is still in the 30-day log window and contact WCPOS support; the export lets support trace the request loop.
evidence: monorepo#1134 item 2 ruling (2026-08-14): demand path stays uncapped, flood detection only; runaway class monorepo#888

actionHint: Compare with the store, then re-apply the correct values once.
summary: A change on this device clashed with an edit made in your store.
docsBody: Open the record and check which version is correct. The POS keeps both sides safe until the clash is settled — nothing is lost.
troubleshooting: Open the record named in the log entry and compare it with the same record in WP Admin.
Decide which version is right — the till's or the store's — and re-apply the correct values once; the POS keeps both sides safe, and further edits to that record are held until the clash is settled.
Frequent conflicts on the same records usually mean two people edit the same data in parallel; agree on where each kind of edit happens.

actionHint: Stop — confirm the charge and settle to the store's total before the customer leaves.
summary: Your store calculated different totals for this order than the till showed.
docsBody: Check the order in your store admin before taking any further payment — the store's totals are the source of truth. If the difference is unexpected, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Stop before taking any further payment — the store's totals are the source of truth.
Open the order in WP Admin and compare its totals with what the till showed; the log entry records which amounts diverged.

The usual causes are tax settings that differ from what the till expected, or a discount or pricing plugin recalculating on the server. If the difference is a tax amount, review the store's tax settings first.
If money was taken for the till's amount and the store says different, settle the difference (refund or additional charge) through your normal process before the customer leaves.
If the divergence is unexplained, export debug info and contact support with the order number.

actionHint: Keep working; reload once if scans keep missing.
summary: Barcode scanning settings could not be loaded, so scans may not match products.
docsBody: The POS keeps trying to load these settings in the background. If scanning stays unreliable, reload the app once.
troubleshooting: Keep working — the POS retries loading the barcode settings in the background.
If scans keep matching nothing, reload the app once.
If it persists after a reload, the settings request itself is failing: check the connection to the store and look for matching errors in Store health → Logs.

actionHint: Wait a moment; reload once if it persists.
summary: Syncing is taking longer than expected to start.
docsBody: This usually resolves by itself within a minute. If the app stays in this state, reload it once before anything else.
troubleshooting: Give it a minute — the first sync after an update, or on a large store, legitimately takes longer.
If the app stays in this state, reload it once.
If slow starts happen daily, check the connection quality to the store and the store's own responsiveness.

actionHint: Nothing to do — one tab syncs for all.
summary: This browser lets only one tab send changes at a time.
docsBody: You can keep using every tab — they all share the same local data. One tab quietly handles the syncing for all of them.
troubleshooting: Keep using every tab normally — they share the same local data, and one tab quietly syncs on behalf of the rest.
This browser (or a private window) lacks the tab-coordination feature the POS prefers, so it falls back to a single syncing tab. No fix is needed.

actionHint: Re-enter the username and password.
summary: The store did not accept the sign-in credentials.
docsBody: Re-enter the username and password, or reset the password in WordPress if it keeps failing. No order data is affected.
troubleshooting: Re-enter the username and password — the store refused this pair.
Confirm the account works by signing in to WP Admin in a browser with the same credentials; reset the password there if it fails.
If the credentials work in WP Admin but not in the POS, a login-protection or security plugin may be blocking programmatic sign-in — check its settings or ask the site administrator.

actionHint: Sign in with your own account.
summary: The signed-in store account does not match the cashier on this till.
docsBody: Each cashier keeps their own till data, so working under another account can misfile orders. Sign out, then sign in with the cashier's own account.
troubleshooting: The POS signs the session out on its own to protect each cashier's data — no order data is mixed between accounts.
Sign back in with the cashier's own account; working under another account can misfile orders.
If tills are shared between cashiers, make switching accounts part of the handover routine.

actionHint: Ask the site admin to reactivate WooCommerce, then reconnect.
summary: WooCommerce is not active on this site, so WCPOS cannot connect.
docsBody: WCPOS requires the WooCommerce plugin. Ask the site administrator to install or reactivate WooCommerce, then connect again.
troubleshooting: Ask the site administrator to check WP Admin → Plugins: WooCommerce must be installed and active for WCPOS to connect.
If WooCommerce was deactivated by a failed update, reactivate it and watch for an error banner — WooCommerce → Status → Logs records why it failed.
Once WooCommerce is active again, reconnect from the till.

actionHint: Ask the site admin to update the WCPOS plugin on the store.
summary: This store's WCPOS plugin is too old for this version of the app.
docsBody: The app has been updated but the WCPOS plugin on the store has not, and the two versions no longer work together. Ask whoever manages the site to update the WCPOS plugin in WP Admin, then connect again. Nothing needs to change on the till.
troubleshooting: Update WCPOS on the store: WP Admin → Plugins → update WCPOS to 1.10.0 or later. If WCPOS Pro is installed, update it to a matching version at the same time.
If no update is offered, check WP Admin → Dashboard → Updates; for Pro, an unauthorized updater blocks updates (see LICENSE301) — fix that first.
After updating, reconnect from the till — you do not need to type the store address again.
If the store cannot be updated yet, contact support: the till needs an app version that matches the plugin, and support can tell you which one.
evidence: monorepo: 1.9.x plugin exposes wcpos/v1 only; client requires wcpos/v2

actionHint: Check the store address for typos.
summary: The store address is missing or not a valid URL.
docsBody: Check the address for typos and include the full https:// URL of the store's WordPress site, then try again.
troubleshooting: Check the address for typos and enter the full URL including https:// — for example https://shop.example.com.
Use the site's WordPress address, not an admin page or a checkout URL.
If the site lives in a subdirectory (for example /shop), include it.

actionHint: Ask your host to let the Authorization header reach WordPress.
summary: The store's server is blocking the login token on every channel this app can use.
docsBody: The app confirmed the store is reachable, but the server (or a firewall, proxy, or security plugin in front of it) strips the Authorization header and also blocks the token when it is sent as a URL parameter. There is no third way to deliver a login token, so this must be fixed on the server.
troubleshooting: Ask your host to allow the Authorization header through to WordPress — on Apache this is usually one line: SetEnvIf Authorization "(.*)" HTTP_AUTHORIZATION=$1.
If the site uses .htaccess rewrites, keep WordPress's generated RewriteRule line that passes HTTP_AUTHORIZATION — security plugins sometimes remove it.
Behind a proxy or CDN, check its header allow-list: the Authorization request header must be forwarded to the origin.
If a web application firewall (WAF) is filtering URL parameters, ask the host to allow the authorization parameter on /wcpos/ REST routes.

actionHint: Ask your host to allow the store's REST API through.
summary: The store's REST API did not answer on any address form this app can use.
docsBody: The app tried the store's REST API at its normal address (/wp-json/...) and at WordPress's built-in fallback address (/?rest_route=...), and neither answered. The store's website itself may be up — this is specifically the REST API being unreachable, usually a security plugin hiding it or a firewall rule blocking it.
troubleshooting: If a security plugin hides or renames /wp-json/ (for example WP Hide), allow WordPress's built-in /?rest_route= form as well — the app falls back to it automatically.
Check firewall (WAF) rules for anything matching wp-json or rest_route and allow the store's own REST API through.
Test from a browser: https://your-store.com/?rest_route=/ should return JSON, not a 403 page or the site's homepage.
If the server is behind a maintenance page or bot challenge, REST requests may be answered with an HTML page — disable the challenge for the REST API.

actionHint: Ask your host to raise the header and URL size limit.
summary: The login token is larger than this server accepts.
docsBody: The server rejected the login token for size: a 400 when it travels in the Authorization header, or a 414 when it travels in the URL. No client-side encoding can shrink it — the server's header/URL size limits must be raised, or the token made smaller.
troubleshooting: On Apache, raise LimitRequestFieldSize (header path) or LimitRequestLine (URL path) in the vhost config.
On nginx, raise large_client_header_buffers.
Behind a proxy or CDN, the limit may be at that layer — check both.
If limits cannot change, contact support about issuing a smaller token for this site.

actionHint: Ask your host to allow the API's OPTIONS preflight.
summary: The server is blocking the browser's permission check (CORS preflight), so the web app cannot reach it.
docsBody: Browsers send an OPTIONS request before any cross-origin API call that carries custom headers. Something in front of this store — usually a firewall rule — is blocking OPTIONS, so the browser never sends the real request. Native apps are unaffected; the fix is server-side.
troubleshooting: Check the firewall (WAF) for a rule blocking the OPTIONS method and allow it on /wcpos/ REST routes.
Some security plugins have a 'block uncommon request methods' toggle — OPTIONS must stay allowed.
Test: an OPTIONS request to the store's REST API should not return 403.
The desktop and mobile apps do not use CORS and will still work while this is being fixed.

actionHint: Ask your host to fix the store's CORS headers.
summary: The server's cross-origin (CORS) configuration is broken, so the browser refuses its responses.
docsBody: The store answers, but its CORS response headers are wrong — duplicated, set to the wrong origin, or missing on error responses. The browser then hides the real answer from the web app, which also masks every other error behind a generic network failure. The fix is server-side: exactly one Access-Control-Allow-Origin, present on every status code.
troubleshooting: Look for a second CORS layer (a plugin AND the server config both adding headers) and remove one — duplicated Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a fatal browser error.
On nginx, add_header lines skip error responses unless they end with 'always' — CORS headers must be on 4xx/5xx too.
If a CDN or proxy adds CORS headers, make sure it does not conflict with WordPress's own.
The desktop and mobile apps do not use CORS and will still work while this is being fixed.

actionHint: Ask your host to allow-list the store's API paths.
summary: A bot-protection page is answering instead of the store's API.
docsBody: The store's REST API is returning an HTML challenge page (bot protection, CAPTCHA, or DDoS interstitial) where the app expects JSON. A point-of-sale app cannot solve a browser challenge; the store's REST API needs to be allow-listed in the protection service.
troubleshooting: Identify the protection layer from the challenge page (Cloudflare, Sucuri, Kinsta and others each brand theirs) and open its settings.
Allow-list the store's own REST API paths (/wp-json/ and /?rest_route=) for API traffic.
On Cloudflare, Bot Fight Mode cannot be bypassed per-path — use Super Bot Fight Mode's 'definitely automated' allow rules or disable it for this zone.
On Kinsta, enable the /wp-json/ allow toggle; on Sucuri, avoid the JavaScript-challenge DDoS mode for API routes.

actionHint: Ask your host to raise the proxy's header limit.
summary: A proxy in front of the store rejects the server's responses for having too many headers.
docsBody: A cache or proxy layer (commonly Varnish) enforces a limit on response header count or size. The store's lightweight endpoints fit, but full API responses exceed the limit and come back as 503s from the proxy, not from WordPress. The limit must be raised on that layer.
troubleshooting: On Varnish, raise http_max_hdr (header count) and http_resp_hdr_len / http_resp_size (sizes).
Ask the host which proxy layer returns the 503 — the WordPress error log will show nothing because the request never fails there.
A quick check: the store's /wcpos/v2/ping answers fine while data endpoints 503.

actionHint: Ask your host to allow product-search requests.
summary: The host's security filter is blocking product searches.
docsBody: A firewall rule on this host rejects REST requests whose query string contains non-ASCII characters or SQL-looking words. Product names with accents, and searches containing words like 'select' or 'union', will fail with a 403 even though they are ordinary catalogue searches. The till works otherwise; searches will be unreliable until the rule is relaxed.
troubleshooting: Ask the host to allow-list the store's own REST search parameters (/wcpos/ and /wc/ routes) in the query-string firewall rules.
On OWASP CRS-based firewalls, the SQL-injection rules on the 's' and 'search' arguments are the usual culprits — exclude those arguments for REST API routes.
Security plugins with a 'filter suspicious query strings' toggle need an exception for the REST API, not a global off switch.

actionHint: Ask your host to exclude the API from caching.
summary: A cache in front of the store is replaying one person's API responses to everyone.
docsBody: A caching layer is serving stored REST API responses without checking who is asking: the app sent two differently-authenticated probes and received the first probe's answer both times. On a live store this means one cashier could see another's data, so connecting is blocked until the cache excludes the store's API. This is a hosting-layer problem — WordPress itself always answers per-user.
troubleshooting: Exclude the store's REST API paths (/wp-json/ and /?rest_route=) from page caching — on LiteSpeed disable REST caching or add a no-cache rule; on WP Engine extend the WooCommerce exclusion to /wp-json/wcpos; on Sucuri set the caching level to honor Cache-Control.
The store's API already sends Cache-Control: no-store and Vary: Authorization — the cache layer is ignoring them; point the host at those headers.
After changing cache settings, purge the cache before reconnecting.

actionHint: Ask your host to raise or exempt the API rate limit.
summary: The host is rate-limiting this store's tills.
docsBody: The server keeps answering 429 (too many requests) even though the app is already backing off and honoring the server's Retry-After delays. Several tills on one internet connection share one address, so per-source rate limits treat them as a single very busy client. Syncing continues automatically but will lag until the limit is raised.
troubleshooting: Ask the host to raise or exempt the REST API rate limit for the store's own traffic — name the shop's static IP if it has one.
Security services that count 30x responses toward a block (for example Sucuri's IDS) may need the store's API excluded from that counter.
If several tills share one connection, mention that to the host: one IP here is a whole shop, not one user.

actionHint: Confirm the request succeeded; ask the admin to check for PHP notices.
summary: Your store sent a malformed response that WCPOS had to repair before reading.
docsBody: This usually means a plugin or PHP notice is printing extra output into store responses. WCPOS recovered this one, but repairs are not guaranteed — ask the site administrator to check the site's error log.
troubleshooting: Check whether the related request ultimately succeeded. If it did, WCPOS repaired this occurrence; if it failed, follow that request's error and retry guidance instead.
The cause is on the site: a plugin or theme is printing warnings or stray output into REST responses. Ask the site administrator to check the site's logs for PHP notices at the failure time.
The network inspector shows the raw response body — the stray output is visible immediately before or after the JSON.
Repairs are best-effort: if these warnings become frequent, fix the offending plugin rather than relying on the repair.

actionHint: Restart WCPOS.
summary: The local database on this device stopped responding, so actions that need it are paused.
docsBody: Restart WCPOS to reconnect the local database. Unsaved changes on this device may not have been written; check recent orders after restarting. If it keeps happening, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Restart WCPOS — closing and reopening the app (or the browser tab) reconnects the local database in almost all cases.
After restarting, check the most recent orders: a change made in the seconds before the failure may not have been written.
On web, avoid private/incognito windows and aggressive storage-cleaning extensions — both can tear down local storage mid-session.
If this returns regularly on the same device, export debug info and contact support, noting what the device was doing (sleep, tab switch, low memory) when it happened.

actionHint: Free up device storage, then restart.
summary: A local database on this device could not be created or removed.
docsBody: Restart WCPOS and try again. If it keeps failing, the device may be low on storage or the browser profile may be restricting storage; free up space, then contact support if it persists.
troubleshooting: Restart WCPOS and try the same action again — most setup failures are transient.
Check free storage on the device; creating a local database fails outright when the disk or the browser's storage quota is full.
On web, check that the browser allows persistent storage for the site — private windows and block-all-data settings do not.
If it keeps failing, export debug info and contact support.

actionHint: No action needed unless a screen stays stuck; then reload the app.
summary: One local database operation took far longer than normal to answer, and the app kept waiting for it.
docsBody: A single read or write to the local database on this device went unanswered for far longer than normal, while the database kept answering everything else. Nothing was cancelled and no data was changed — this entry exists so a stuck screen or spinner leaves a trace naming exactly which operation stalled. Stalled sync work is given up on and retried automatically (logged as SYNC321); a stalled call from a screen is not retried, so if it never answers, that screen stays stuck until the app is reloaded.
troubleshooting: If everything is working, no action is needed — the call most likely completed, just slowly. If a change was being saved at the time, open the record and confirm it saved.
If a screen or spinner stays stuck, reload the app (or the browser tab) to abandon the stuck operation and start it again.

If this code returns regularly on the same device, export debug info and contact support; the entry's context names the operation and data collection, the exact wait, and how busy the database was meanwhile.
evidence: 2026-08-25 demo store coupons screen spun forever while every existing signal stayed silent; report-only stall detector added in monorepo#1596

actionHint: Try adding it again; try a different item if it keeps failing.
summary: This change could not be applied to the cart, which is unchanged.
docsBody: The item, fee, shipping line, or coupon was not added and nothing was removed. Try the action again; if it keeps failing, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Try adding the item, fee, shipping line or coupon again — the cart itself is unchanged.
If the same item keeps failing, try a different product once: one failing item points at that record, everything failing points at the device.
If it keeps failing, restart WCPOS; export debug info and contact support if it continues.

actionHint: Search by name; ask the admin to make the barcodes unique.
summary: More than one product matches this barcode.
docsBody: WCPOS cannot pick between them safely, so nothing was added. Search for the product by name, and give each product a unique barcode in the store to fix the clash.
troubleshooting: Search for the product by name to complete this sale — the scan added nothing because the barcode matches more than one product.
The log entry records the scanned code and how many products matched; searching the POS for the barcode value shows which ones they are.
In WP Admin, give each of those products its own unique barcode, then rescan to confirm only one match remains.

actionHint: Ask the admin to re-save the product's prices.
summary: This product's variation price data could not be read, so displayed prices may be wrong or missing.
docsBody: Re-save the product in WooCommerce to rebuild its price data, or contact support if many products show this.
troubleshooting: Open the product in WP Admin and re-save it — this rebuilds the price data the POS could not read.
Check that each of the product's variations has a price set; a variation without a price produces unreadable price ranges.
If many products show this code at once, a pricing plugin is likely writing price data in a format the POS cannot read — note which plugin manages prices and contact support.

actionHint: Retry; check the email/SMTP or download settings.
summary: This receipt could not be emailed or downloaded.
docsBody: The sale itself is unaffected. Check the email address and the device's connection, then try again from the order's receipt screen.
troubleshooting: Expand the log entry to identify the delivery path: an email address or server status identifies email delivery; a templateId without an email identifies PDF generation, download, save or sharing.
For email delivery, check the address and connection, then resend from the order's receipt screen. If every email fails, ask the site administrator to check outgoing email and SMTP configuration.
For a PDF failure, retry Download PDF, check the device's free storage and download permissions, then choose a writable save location or another available share target.

actionHint: Pause a moment, confirm your last action went through, then retry.
summary: WCPOS queued too many requests at once and dropped some.
docsBody: This is usually an app defect rather than a store problem. Restart WCPOS; if the code returns, export diagnostics and contact support.
troubleshooting: Pause for a few seconds — the queue drains on its own and stale requests are dropped automatically — then retry the action.
If it happens again in the same session, restart WCPOS; the queue clears on restart.
This is usually an app defect rather than a store problem: if it keeps returning, export debug info and contact support — the entry's context tells the developers which requests flooded the queue.

actionHint: No action needed. If search results still look wrong, reload the app.
summary: Local search returned results that do not match the catalogue; the app attempts an automatic search index rebuild.
docsBody: WCPOS detected results that did not match the search term. The mismatched results are hidden and the app attempts to rebuild the local search index automatically. No catalogue data was changed.
troubleshooting: Usually no action is needed: mismatched results are hidden and the index is rebuilt automatically. If search results still look wrong, reload the app.
If the code returns, export debug info and contact support; the log context identifies the affected catalogue and search.
evidence: confirmed field incident: in-memory search results diverged from catalogue documents

actionHint: No action needed. Search keeps working from a direct catalogue scan.
summary: The search index did not answer in time, so WCPOS searched the catalogue directly instead.
docsBody: The local search index was still building or could not run — typically when the POS tab has been in the background or another tab holds the database lead. Searches still answer, from a direct scan of the local catalogue, and switch back to the index automatically once it responds. No catalogue data was changed.
troubleshooting: Usually no action is needed: search results keep working and the index takes over again on its own.
If this code appears on every search all day, keep the POS in its own browser window rather than a background tab, and reload the app once.
If the code returns after a reload, export debug info and contact support; the log context identifies the affected catalogue.
evidence: monorepo#1733 silent zero-result searches while the index pipeline was stalled

actionHint: No action needed. If search still misses products you can see in the catalogue, reload the app.
summary: The search index could not find a product it should contain; the app attempts an automatic search index rebuild.
docsBody: A periodic self-check asked the local search index for a product by that product's own name and the index did not return it. That means searches may have been showing fewer results than the catalogue really holds. The app attempts to rebuild the local search index automatically. No catalogue data was changed.
troubleshooting: Usually no action is needed: the index is rebuilt automatically and searches recover on their own.
If search still misses products you can see in the catalogue, reload the app to rebuild the in-memory index.
If the code returns, export debug info and contact support; the log context identifies the affected catalogue and the sample the index missed.
evidence: monorepo#1733 divergence detector was one-sided: false hits were detected, false misses never were

actionHint: Reload the app so it can rebuild the search index.
summary: The automatic search index rebuild failed, so search on this device may stay incomplete for the rest of this session.
docsBody: After detecting a search index problem the app tried to rebuild the index, and the rebuild itself failed. Search keeps answering — from the existing index with known bad results hidden, or from a direct scan of the data on this device — but it may miss or misrank results for the affected list. The app attempts only one rebuild per list per session, so it will not retry on its own; reloading the app resets that and lets it try again. No store data was changed.
troubleshooting: Open the log entry — its context names the list affected and the error the rebuild hit. If that error mentions storage, free up space on the device first; on web, also avoid private/incognito windows.
Reload the app (or the browser tab) — a reload lets the app attempt the rebuild again the next time the problem is detected.
If CLIENT144 is logged again after the reload, export debug info and contact support.
evidence: 2026-09-01 log audit: both rebuild-failure paths from monorepo#1733 logged without a code while their sibling detections carried CLIENT141-143

actionHint: Remove that line and add it again, then check the total.
summary: A line on this order has price details the POS could not read, so its amount was taken from the stored totals instead.
docsBody: The line's saved price basis — the price, tax status and tax-inclusive flag the POS records against it — could not be read, so the amount shown was derived from whatever totals were already on the line. Remove the line and add it again to rebuild that data, then check the order total before taking payment.
troubleshooting: Check the order total against what you expect before taking payment — the affected line's amount came from stored totals, not from a recalculated price.
Remove the affected line and add the product, fee or shipping method again; a freshly added line always carries readable price details.
If the line was added on an older version of WCPOS, or restored from a backup, the price details it carries may predate the current format — re-adding it is the fix.
If new lines keep producing this code, export debug info and contact support with the order number: something is writing the POS price data in a format the app cannot read.

actionHint: Check the tax on this order; ask the admin whether a tax rate was deleted.
summary: This order refers to a tax rate your store no longer has, so its tax may be wrong.
docsBody: A line on the order carries a tax rate id that is not in the store's current tax tables — usually because the rate was deleted or edited in WooCommerce after the order was started. Check the tax on the order before taking payment, and have whoever manages the store confirm the tax rates.
troubleshooting: Check the tax amount on the order before taking payment — the rate it was calculated with is no longer in your store.
Ask whoever manages the store whether a tax rate was deleted or edited recently; deleting a rate that orders already reference is the usual cause.
Start the sale on a new order once the tax rates are settled — a new order picks up the store's current rates.
If the store's tax rates have not changed, the POS may be holding a stale copy: open Store health and resync tax rates, then export debug info and contact support if the code returns.
